title: Sickle Cell Retinopathy: From Hemoglobinopathy to Sea Fans
summary: Sickle Cell Retinopathy (SCR) is a sight-threatening manifestation of systemic sickling hemoglobinopathies. While HbSS causes severe systemic disease, the ocular manifestations are paradoxically more frequent and severe in HbSC and S-Thal variants due to higher blood viscosity.

sections.title: Clinical Overview & Definition
sections.content: Sickle Cell Retinopathy (SCR) encompasses the ocular changes resulting from vaso-occlusive events in the retinal and choroidal circulation. It is caused by the inheritance of abnormal hemoglobin (HbS), where valine is substituted for glutamic acid at the sixth position of the β-globin chain. This leads to RBC sickling under hypoxic, acidotic, or hyperosmolar conditions.

sections.title: The Pathophysiological Cascade
content: 1. HbS Polymerization: Triggered by hypoxia or acidosis.
2. RBC Sickling: Erythrocytes become rigid and crescent-shaped.
3. Vaso-occlusion: Stasis in peripheral retinal arterioles.
4. Retinal Ischemia: Release of pro-angiogenic factors (VEGF).
5. Proliferative Retinopathy: Neovascular 'Sea Fan' formation.

rows: A-V shunts at the junction of perfused and non-perfused retina.
The 'Sea Fan' stage; often at the border of ischemia.
Bleeding from fragile sea fan vessels into the vitreous cavity.
Tractional or rhegmatogenous (secondary to breaks near traction).

sections.title: Anterior Segment & Unique Findings
content: Conjunctival Comma Sign: Isolated vascular segments on the bulbar conjunctiva.
Iris Ischemia: Can present as sectoral atrophy or even rubeosis iridis.
Hyphema Danger: Sickled cells clog the trabecular meshwork rapidly, raising IOP.
Angioid Streaks: Occur in up to 6% of patients (calcification of Bruch's membrane).

sections.title: Macular Manifestations
content: Sickle Maculopathy: Chronic ischemia leads to thinning of the inner retinal layers.
Vascular Changes: Enlarged Foveal Avascular Zone (FAZ) on OCT-A.
Macular Depression Sign: Oval depression due to focal atrophy.
Peripheral-to-Central Progression: Macula is usually spared until late stages.

rows: Idiopathic peripheral perivasculitis, usually bilateral, male predominance.
History of prematurity, bilateral, lack of 'salmon patches'.
Microaneurysms, hard exudates, posterior pole involvement initially.
Massive exudation, telangiectatic 'light bulb' vessels, usually unilateral.

sections.title: Investigation & Imaging Workup
content: 1. DFE: Wide-field fundus examination is mandatory.
2. Hemoglobin Electrophoresis: To confirm Hb variant (SS, SC, S-Thal).
3. Wide-field FFA: Gold standard to identify 'Sea Fans' and peripheral non-perfusion.
4. OCT-A: Non-invasive detection of macular and peripheral capillary drop-out.
5. B-scan USG: Indicated if Vitreous Hemorrhage obscures the view.

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Observation: For Stages I and II, and small Stage III fans (high autoinfarction rate).
Scatter Laser Photocoagulation: Target the peripheral ischemic zone (not the fans directly).
Feeder Vessel Treatment: Historically used but high risk of VH and retinal breaks.
Anti-VEGF: Temporary regression of sea fans; used as adjunct to surgery/laser.
Pars Plana Vitrectomy: Reserved for non-clearing VH or TRD.

sections.title: EMERGENCY: Hyphema Management
content: Avoid Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (CAIs): They increase acidity, promoting sickling.
Avoid Hyperosmotics (Mannitol): Increases hemoconcentration and sickling.
Aggressive IOP Control: Lower threshold for surgical washout (IOP > 24 mmHg for 24h).
Use Beta-Blockers and Alpha-Agonists: Safest options for IOP reduction.

sections.title: Surgical Considerations (PPV)
content: Pre-op Exchange Transfusion: Consider to reduce HbS levels below 30%.
Avoid Scleral Buckling: High risk of anterior segment ischemia (ASI).
Intraoperative Hydration: Vital to prevent sickling crises.
Monitor for Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG) post-operatively.

content.explanation: Occlusion (1), Anastomoses (2), Neovascularization (3), Vitreous Heme (4), Detachment (5).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Autoinfarction: Sea fans may spontaneously regress (withered sea fan) in up to 25% of cases.
Peripheral Predominance: SCR is primarily a disease of the temporal periphery.
Higher Hematocrit = Higher Risk: This is why HbSC (higher Hct than HbSS) is more ocularly dangerous.
Systemic Screening: All patients with sickle cell disease should have annual dilated exams starting at age 10.

sections.title: Landmark Insights
sections.content: Evidence from the Sickle Cell Retinopathy Study group suggests that while laser photocoagulation effectively regresses neovascularization and reduces the incidence of vitreous hemorrhage, it does not significantly change the long-term visual acuity outcome compared to observation for most patients, unless advanced proliferative disease is present.
